title: Svastidā viśaspatiḥ: may Indra, giver of well-being, go before us
theme: Indra — giver of well-being, lord of the people, slayer of Vṛtra, repeller of foes, the controller, the bull — is asked to go before the speakers as the maker of fearlessness.

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «स्वस्तिदा भूलोकसुखकृत्» — who makes happiness in this world
The anonymous commentator: «विशो नानाविधप्रजायाः पतिः प्रभुः» — master of the many kinds of creatures
The anonymous commentator: «विमृधो रक्षोजातिमथनकर्ता» — who crushes the race of rakṣases
The anonymous commentator: «वशी त्रैलोक्यवशीकारवान्» — who holds the three worlds in his power
The anonymous commentator: «वृषा प्रावृषि वृष्ट्युदकसेचकः» — who pours the rain in the rainy season
The anonymous commentator: «स्वस्तिदा आमुत्रिकसुखकृत्» — the second time: who makes happiness in the other world
The anonymous commentator: «अभयंकरः स्वाश्रितानाम्» — for those who take refuge in him

sandhi.type: visarga after ā before a voiced consonant; after i before a voiced consonant
sandhi.rule: svastidāḥ before v drops its visarga; viśaspatiḥ before v becomes viśaspatir.

sandhi.type: visarga after a before a voiced consonant

sandhi.rule: ā + i becomes e: vṛṣā indraḥ → vṛṣendraḥ.

sandhi.type: visarga after a before a vowel other than a
sandhi.rule: puraḥ before e drops its visarga and stands in hiatus.

sandhi.type: visarga before s; visarga after ā before a vowel
sandhi.rule: naḥ before s is written nas s (the recitation text’s doubled sibilant); svastidāḥ before a drops its visarga and stands in hiatus.

morphology.note: A compound that keeps the genitive of its first member, viśaḥ, with the visarga written s before p: viśas-patiḥ, ‘lord of the people’. The edition keeps it as one word.
The first member abhaya keeps a nasal before kara (abhayaṃ-kara), written ṅ before k.

translation.literal: Giver of well-being, lord of the people, slayer of Vṛtra, repeller of foes, the controller — may the bull Indra go before us, giver of well-being, maker of fearlessness.
translation.readable: May Indra go before us: giver of well-being, lord of the people, slayer of Vṛtra, driver-off of enemies, master of all, the showering bull, the one who makes us unafraid.

anvaya: स्वस्तिदाः विशस्पतिः वृत्रहा विमृधः वशी वृषा अभयङ्करः स्वस्तिदाः इन्द्रः नः पुरः एतु ।
syntax: A single sentence: the subject indraḥ with eight epithets in the nominative, svastidāḥ framing the verse at its beginning and near its end, and the imperative etu with the adverb puraḥ and the genitive naḥ.

ambiguities.note: The epithet is repeated. The commentator gives each its own sense: well-being in this world and in the other, «स्वस्तिदा भूलोकसुखकृत्। पुनः स्वस्तिदा आमुत्रिकसुखकृत्».

metre.name: anuṣṭubh
metre.note: As printed 15 + 16 syllables: svastidā viśaspatir (7) vṛtrahā vimṛdho vaśī (8); vṛṣendraḥ pura etu nas (8) svastidā abhayaṅkaraḥ (8). The first pāda has seven; reading svasti with su as two syllables (suvasti) would give eight, but the edition only reports the count.

beginner: This prayer asks Indra, the king of the gods, to go in front of the speakers, as a leader goes before a band of travellers. It piles up his titles: giver of well-being, lord of the people, the one who killed the serpent Vṛtra, the one who drives off enemies, the one who rules everything, the bull who brings rain, and the one who makes people unafraid. "Giver of well-being" comes twice; the old commentator says the first time means well-being in this world and the second in the next. He explains the request as protection on every side, so that, guarded by Indra, the travellers may be without fear. The edition reports what the words and the commentator say; it makes no claim about what reciting the prayer brings.
analogy: Like a guide walking ahead of a group through unknown country: those behind can go without fear because someone they trust goes first.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It asks Indra to go before the speakers, naming him giver of well-being, lord of the people, slayer of Vṛtra, repeller of foes, controller, bull and maker of fearlessness.

commentary.q: How does the commentator read ‘go before us’?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator: for those who travel here and there, may Indra come before them to protect them, and by extension in every direction: «इतस्ततो गच्छतां नोऽस्माकं पुरः पुरस्तादौपलक्षण्येन प्रागवाक्प्रत्यगुदगूर्ध्वाधोदिक्षु परिपालनायेन्द्र एत्वागच्छतु». The point: «सर्वतो दिक्षु वज्रहस्तेन पालिता वयं निर्भयाः स्यामेति भावः» — guarded on every side by the one who holds the thunderbolt, may we be without fear.

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this anuvāka is in the edition’s sources (Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not among them). The anonymous bhāṣya explains the words and the rite; it does not argue an Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita or Dvaita position here, so the edition gives none.

contemporary.text: The prayer does not ask for the road to be safe; it asks for someone to walk ahead. Courage often comes less from removing danger than from not facing it alone. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Who has ‘gone before’ you, making a hard road easier to walk?
reflect.deeper: Why might the prayer name so many titles before making its single request?
reflect.practice: Go ahead of someone in one small difficulty today, so that they can follow without fear.

references.text: No comment of Sāyaṇa’s or Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara’s on this anuvāka is in the edition’s sources: Sāyaṇa’s anuvākas 52–57 are missing from the digital text used here, and neither commentary file glosses these words; the edition’s concordance maps give no anuvāka of theirs for it. The anonymous bhāṣya is the only commentary quoted.
A verse very close to this one is in the Ṛgveda (10.152.2), whose last pāda differs. The edition’s Ṛgveda source has only the first maṇḍala, so the parallel is noted here, not quoted.
